description_ru: Оахака в День мёртвых: кладбищенские пикники, алтари-офренды, процессии с оркестрами и неожиданно светлый разговор о смерти.
text:
I arrived in Oaxaca on the thirtieth of October, a day too early for anything to happen and therefore perfectly timed. The city, in the south of Mexico, was already in the grip of what felt like a prolonged, joyful rehearsal. Marigolds were stacked in the market in orange mountains, and the air smelled of copal incense, hot chocolate and woodsmoke. Street vendors were selling sugar skulls with names iced across the forehead. In the zócalo, the main square, a small girl in a skeleton costume was solemnly directing traffic, which, given the local standard of driving, seemed a reasonable intervention.

The Day of the Dead, celebrated on the first and second of November, is easily the most misunderstood festival in the world. Visitors from colder, tidier countries tend to expect something macabre, a sort of Mexican Halloween. It is nothing of the sort. The festival has roots in Indigenous traditions that long predate the arrival of the Spanish, and over the centuries these have blended with Catholic observances to produce something entirely its own. The central belief, as it was explained to me by the owner of my guesthouse, a gentle, brisk woman called Marisol, is that the dead are not gone. Once a year, they are permitted to return and be fed.

Marisol took me to the market to buy what she needed for her family's ofrenda, the altar built in the home for the returning souls. The ingredients, I discovered, were both specific and deeply personal. There was pan de muerto, a sweet bread decorated with strips of dough in the shape of bones. There were candles, a bowl of water for the thirsty traveller, and a path of marigold petals, called cempasúchil, whose scent is believed to guide the spirits home. And there was, for Marisol's grandfather, a small glass of mezcal, a bar of dark chocolate, and a packet of the cigarettes he had smoked until the day he died. "He would be furious if we forgot them," she said, grinning. "He was a difficult man. We loved him."

On the evening of the first, I walked to the cemetery in the village of Xoxocotlán, expecting solemnity. What I found was something closer to a vast, candlelit picnic. Families had gathered around the graves, which were covered with flowers and glowing with thousands of candles, and they were eating, drinking, chatting in low voices and, here and there, singing. Children darted between the headstones. Old women sat on folding chairs, wrapped in shawls, keeping a long vigil with the calm of people who had done it all their lives. Nobody minded my presence, although I tried to stay discreetly at the margin, and a man who noticed me hovering silently pressed a cup of hot, spiced ponche into my hands.

I remember thinking how different this was from our own, rather embarrassed, relationship with death. In much of Europe, we handle mortality with euphemism and a certain brisk avoidance. Here, the dead were treated as honoured guests, with their own tastes and quirks and favourite songs. People spoke of them in the present tense. Standing in that field of candles, I found that I was less afraid of the subject than I had been in years, and that surprised me more than the marigolds.

The following day, the city staged its comparsas, boisterous processions in which brass bands, dancers and neighbours in elaborate costumes parade through the streets. Many wore skeleton makeup, painstakingly applied, and some carried lanterns and puppets of enormous size. A brass band played a tune that was half funeral march and half wedding, and a man dressed as a bride, complete with a beard, danced down the middle of the road with a bottle of mezcal. Humour is central to the tradition. Skeletons are shown laughing, flirting, riding bicycles, and playing the guitar. The idea is that death, being universal, is best met with a smile.

Between ceremonies, I spent my days eating, which is the only intelligent way to visit Oaxaca. The state is renowned as the land of seven moles, rich sauces of chilli, chocolate, nuts and spices, of which the black version, mole negro, can take days to prepare. I ate it over chicken in a courtyard shaded by bougainvillea, and it tasted of smoke, bitter chocolate and some deep, undefinable sweetness. In another café, I tried tlayudas, enormous crisp tortillas piled with beans and cheese, and chapulines, toasted grasshoppers seasoned with lime and chilli. They taste, if you must know, like very crunchy, very savoury crisps.

On my final night, Marisol called me into her kitchen, where the family had assembled around the ofrenda. The candles flickered over photographs of people I would never meet. She handed me a small piece of bread and asked me, a little shyly, whether I would like to say something for my own dead. I hesitated, feeling like an impostor. Then I thought of my grandmother, who had died years before and had a notorious weakness for marmalade, and I said a few words aloud, in English, to a room of strangers who nodded gravely as if they understood every one.

It was, without question, the most moving moment of my travels. I left the next morning with a bag of sugar skulls and the strange sensation of having been, for a few days, in the company of more people than I could see.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: morˈtality, ˈeuphemism, interˈvention. В словах на -ity ударение падает на слог перед -ity.
Дифтонг «ɔɪ»: от «о» к «и»: boisterous. Не заменяйте на простое «ой» без скольжения.
Дифтонг «əʊ» (брит.) или «oʊ» (америк.): от краткого «ə» к «у»; губы округляются к концу: own, ofrenda.
Глухие «k», «t», «p» перед ударным гласным придыхательные: candles, cemetery — лёгкий выдох после согласного.

questions.question: When is the Day of the Dead celebrated?
questions.answer: On the first and second of November.

questions.question: What is an ofrenda?
questions.answer: An altar built at home for the returning souls of the dead.

questions.question: What did the writer find in the cemetery at Xoxocotlán?
questions.answer: A candlelit gathering where families ate, drank and sang beside the graves.

questions.question: How does the writer compare Mexican and European attitudes to death?
questions.answer: Europeans use euphemism and avoidance, while in Oaxaca the dead are honoured guests.
